title: Training & Outreach
text:
RaukR

Since 2018, together with Sebastian DiLorenzo, Roy Francis and other NBIS colleagues, I organise RaukR, the Advanced R Programming for Bioinformatics summer school held on the island of Gotland in Visby, Sweden. The course covers writing robust, efficient and reproducible R for life-science data. Course materials and information about upcoming editions are at raukr.nbis.se.
Over the years, RaukR has hosted guest instructors from the R community, including Martin Morgan, Paula Moraga, Max Kuhn, Yihui Xie, Richard Iannone, Christophe Dervieux, Jenny Bryan and Henrik Bengtsson.

Talks and popular science

From mythology to artificial intelligence: a short journey through statistical models (in Swedish: Från mytologi till artificiell intelligens. En kort resa genom statistiska modeller)

Public lecture in the 13x13 series, Uppsala University, 5 November 2025, Humanistiska Teatern. The talk follows how people have tried to understand the world, from myth to modern statistical models and AI: how such models are built, how reliable they are, and what to look out for when a new AI model appears. 13x13 is a series of thirteen free lectures, organised by the Department of Physics and Astronomy, in which Uppsala researchers present their work to a general audience.

title: Pest in R using R6 classes
text:
Hello! In this post, I will show you how one can implement an agent-based simulation in R using object-oriented programming paradigm (OOP) and R6 classes.
This simulation is working yet it still has to be polished. It has been implemented as a live coding demo during “OOP in R” session at RaukR 2024.
Our goal is to simulate epidemics dynamics on an island (an isolated world). Let us establish some simple rules:

title: Pest in R using R6 classes
Pest in R using R6 classes
Pest in R using R6 classes
text:
Auxiliary functions
I have written a function that visualizes states of our world as the simulation goes on using ggplot2 and gganimate packages. Here is the code:

visualize_simulation <- function(results) {
  p <- ggplot(results, aes(x = col, y = row)) +
    geom_tile(aes(fill = sick)) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "red") +
    theme_minimal() +
    labs(title = "Disease Spread Simulation", x = "X", y = "Y", fill = "Sick Individuals") +
    transition_states(step, transition_length = 2, state_length = 1) +
    ease_aes('linear') +
    ggtitle('Disease Spread Simulation - Generation {closest_state}') +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5))
  
  animate(p, nframes = length(unique(results$step)), fps = 2, renderer = gifski_renderer())
}

title: Pest in R using R6 classes
text:
Running simulation
Now, we need a function that will enable us to run the simulation:

library(ggplot2)
library(gganimate)
library(progress)

run_simulation <- function(size, num_steps, initial_healthy, initial_immune, initial_sick, beta, recovery_prob, death_prob) {
  stopifnot(recovery_prob + death_prob <= 1) # some simplistic input validation
  pb <- progress_bar$new(total = num_steps + 1)
  
  world <- World$new(size)
  
  # Initialize agents
  if (initial_healthy > 0) {
    for (i in 1:initial_healthy) {
      row <- sample(1:size, 1)
      col <- sample(1:size, 1)
      world$add_agent(row, col, Agent$new())
    }
  }
  
  # Introduce immune and sick agents
  if (initial_immune > 0) {
    for (i in 1:initial_immune) {
      row <- sample(1:size, 1)
      col <- sample(1:size, 1)
      world$add_agent(row, col, Agent$new(state = "immune"))
    }
  }
  
  if (initial_sick > 0) {
    for (i in 1:initial_sick) {
      row <- sample(1:size, 1)
      col <- sample(1:size, 1)
      world$add_agent(row, col, Agent$new(state = "sick"))
    }
  }
  
  results <- list()
  
  # Save the initial state of the world
  counts <- world$get_counts()
  counts$step <- 1
  results[[1]] <- counts
  
  
  # Simulate one generation
  for (step in 2:num_steps + 1) {
    world$update_states(beta, recovery_prob, death_prob)
    world$move_agents()
    counts <- world$get_counts()
    counts$step <- step
    results[[step]] <- counts
    pb$tick()
  }
  
  results <- do.call(rbind, results)
  
  return(results)
}

Finally, we can run our simulation:

library(tidyverse)

# Parameters
size <- 20                    # World size
num_steps <- 50               # Number of generations
initial_healthy <- 998
initial_immune <- 0
initial_sick <- 2
beta <- 0.5                  # Transmission probability
recovery_prob <- 0.1
death_prob <- 0.05

# Run the simulation
results <- run_simulation(size, num_steps, initial_healthy, initial_immune, initial_sick, beta, recovery_prob, death_prob)

results |> group_by(step) |> 
  summarise(n_sick = sum(sick), n_healthy = sum(healthy), n_immune = sum(immune), n_dead = sum(dead)) |> 
  pivot_longer(starts_with("n_"), names_to = 'measure') |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = step, y = value, col=measure)) + geom_line() + theme_minimal()

title: Making more glamorous graphs in ggplot2
text:
NoteUpdated in 2026



Lightly edited from a 2020 post. The plot is re-rendered with current packages (size became linewidth in ggplot2). The data stop in February 2020, and the scraper is shown but not run, since the repository pages it parsed have changed.
Inspired by William R. Chase’s rstudio::conf 2020 talk “The Glamour of Graphics”, I decided to spruce up an old plot. It is the one I show my students every year to motivate them to learn R: the number of R packages available in various repositories over the years.
From William’s talk I took these lessons:
There is much more in the talk that I do not implement here, for example using professional fonts.

title: Making more glamorous graphs in ggplot2
text:
Data
I have an ugly function that scrapes CRAN, R-Forge, Bioconductor and, later, also GitHub to count R packages (GitHub is a bit problematic, but hopefully a good proxy). The function repeats code that I should have encapsulated and parametrised. No one is perfect.

interrogate_repos <- function() {
  # CRAN
  cran_con <- curl::curl(url = 'https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/index.html')
  cran <- paste0(readLines(con = cran_con, n = 20), collapse = '')
  cran_pkgs <- stringr::str_match(cran, 'repository features ([0-9]{1,}) available packages')[2]

  # R-Forge
  rforge_con <- curl::curl(url = 'https://r-forge.r-project.org')
  rforge <- paste0(readLines(con = rforge_con, n = 200), collapse = '')
  rforge_pkgs <- stringr::str_replace(stringr::str_match(rforge, 'Projects: <strong>([0-9]{1,},[0-9]{1,})</strong>')[2], ',', '')

  # Bioconductor
  bioconductor_con <- curl::curl(url = 'https://bioconductor.org')
  bioconductor <- paste0(readLines(con = bioconductor_con, n = 200), collapse = '')
  bioconductor_pkgs <- stringr::str_match(bioconductor, 'Software\">([0-9]{1,}).*software packages.')[2]

  # GitHub
  github_con <- curl::curl(url = 'https://github.com/search?l=R&q=R+package&type=Repositories')
  github <- paste0(readLines(con = github_con, n = 1200), collapse = '')
  github_pkgs <- stringr::str_replace(stringr::str_match(github, '([0-9]{1,},[0-9]{1,}) repository results')[2], ',', '')

  day <- format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%d")
  result <- c(day, cran_pkgs, rforge_pkgs, bioconductor_pkgs, github_pkgs)
  names(result) <- c('date', 'CRAN', 'R-Forge', 'Bioconductor', 'GitHub')
  return(result)
}

From time to time I ran the following code to update my dataset:

prev_data <- read_csv('num_pkgs_data.csv')
today <- interrogate_repos()
if (last(prev_data$date) < today[1]) {
  prev_data <- rbind(prev_data, today)
  write_csv(x = prev_data, 'num_pkgs_data.csv')
}

title: Making more glamorous graphs in ggplot2
Making more glamorous graphs in ggplot2
text:
Plotting
I needed some cool colours. On my way home from rstudio::conf 2020 I watched Taika Waititi’s “Jojo Rabbit”, which I found visually appealing. I grabbed a screenshot and, with the Colormind tool, created two palettes from it.

jojo1 <- c('#c0b3aa', '#2b2117', '#9a8268', '#d3a677', '#e1d0ba')
jojo2 <- c('#221c17', '#947e66', '#da9869', '#e0c6a4', '#c1b3ab')

And now the most glamorous version of the plot, with the legend living in the title:

cols <- c('bioconductor' = jojo2[2], 'cran' = jojo2[3], 'github' = jojo2[1], 'rforge' = jojo2[5])

title <- glue('Log # of R packages available at',
              ' <span style="color:{cols[2]}">**CRAN**</span>,',
              ' <span style="color:{cols[4]}">**R-Forge**</span>,',
              ' <span style="color:{cols[1]}">**Bioconductor**</span>',
              ' and',
              ' <span style="color:{cols[3]}">**GitHub**</span>',
              ' over time.')

ggplot(data, mapping = aes(x = date, y = log(value), col = repo)) +
  geom_point(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_line(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = comma(value)), direction = 'y', vjust = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cols) +
  labs(title = title, x = '', y = '') +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = '#EEEEEE', linewidth = 0.25),
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = '#FFFDF8', colour = '#FFFDF8'),
        axis.title = element_text(colour = jojo2[5]),
        axis.text = element_text(colour = jojo2[5], size = 10),
        axis.title.y = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_markdown(lineheight = 1.5, size = 12),
        plot.title.position = 'plot')

title: Receiving ACARS messages with a software-defined radio on a Mac
text:
NoteFrom the archive



First published on my old blog in September 2014 as Compiling and installing rtl_acars on OS X 10.9 Mavericks. These steps are for a 2014 system and are very likely out of date: the software, the build tools and macOS itself have all changed since. I keep the post for the fun of it.


I struggled for a while, but in the end I managed to install rtl_acars on my Mac, and after some hours of waiting I received my first ACARS messages. ACARS is the short-message system that aircraft use to talk to ground stations. Now it is only a matter of building a better antenna. Here is my path to success.
# Clone 9nut's version of rtl-sdr from GitHub
git clone https://github.com/9nut/rtl-sdr

# Add missing lines in Makefile.am
rtl_acars_SOURCES = rtl_acars.c
rtl_acars_LDADD = librtlsdr.la $(LIBM)

# I had previously installed Homebrew to get the necessary libraries
brew install libtool
aclocal
glibtoolize
autoconf
automake --add-missing

# Choose your own destination
./configure --prefix=/Users/user/rtl/
make
make install

title: Mapping between genome assemblies in R
text:
NoteFrom the archive



First published on my old blog in March 2014. I have kept the idea and the original plyr solution, and added a version with today’s dplyr.
Genome arrays are designed against one particular version of a genome assembly. New assemblies are published, but the array stays the same, so you often need to map between the two. In my case, the task was to map between two assemblies of the canine genome, from canFam2 to CanFam3, for a SNP array. I had two .map files with genomic coordinates per marker, which look like this:
I wanted to join them so that the marker names come from the canFam2 file, while the chromosome and position come from the matching marker in the canFam3 file.

title: Mapping between genome assemblies in R
text:
The pitfall of merge()
The first thing that came to mind was merge(). The problem is that a marker that has no match in canFam3 is moved to the end of the result, which breaks the marker order. What we want instead is NA in both the chromosome and the position when the marker cannot be found in canFam3.

title: Mapping between genome assemblies in R
text:
The solution: a left join
The R package plyr has exactly that, in its join() function:
new.map <- join(map, canFam3, by = "marker", type = "left")
Today the same thing is usually written with dplyr. Here it is with a tiny made-up example, so you can see that the order is preserved and the missing marker gets NA:

library(dplyr)

canFam2 <- data.frame(
  marker = c("BICF2G630707759", "BICF2S2358127", "BICF2P1173580", "BICF2X0000001"),
  chr2 = 1, pos2 = c(14548, 68723, 80040, 90111)
)
canFam3 <- data.frame(
  marker = c("BICF2P1173580", "BICF2G630707759", "BICF2S2358127"),
  chr3 = 1, pos3 = c(81233, 15021, 69300)
)

left_join(canFam2, canFam3, by = "marker")

           marker chr2  pos2 chr3  pos3
1 BICF2G630707759    1 14548    1 15021
2   BICF2S2358127    1 68723    1 69300
3   BICF2P1173580    1 80040    1 81233
4   BICF2X0000001    1 90111   NA    NA


The unmatched marker BICF2X0000001 stays in its place and gets NA for the new coordinates, which is what we wanted. In base R, match() does the same job: canFam3$pos3[match(canFam2$marker, canFam3$marker)].






TipWhen marker names are not shared



This trick works because the same array markers appear in both assemblies. To convert coordinates that have no shared identifiers, use a chain-file based lift-over instead, for example liftOver() in the Bioconductor package rtracklayer.

title: Marcin Kierczak, PhD
text:
Training & Industry Outreach Coordinator · Data Scientist · NBIS

I coordinate training and industry outreach at the National Bioinformatics Infrastructure Sweden (NBIS), part of SciLifeLab, connecting Swedish life science with the bioinformatics skills and expertise it needs. As a data scientist at NBIS, I also work with research groups on their data analysis. In addition, I am an associate professor of bioinformatics at Uppsala University, with a research background in machine learning, statistical genomics and ancient DNA.

Formulas in the background
Some pages show faint, slowly drifting formulas behind the text. They are decoration, but each one is real:


Show the formulas and what they mean








Formula
What it is




\(\mathrm{softmax}(z)_i = \dfrac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}\)
Softmax. Turns a vector of raw scores into probabilities that sum to 1; the last step of most classifiers.


\(P(\theta \mid D) = \dfrac{P(D \mid \theta)\,P(\theta)}{P(D)}\)
Bayes’ theorem. Updates belief about parameters \(\theta\) after seeing data \(D\): posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence.


\(\mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, \sigma^2) = (2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\dfrac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\)
Normal distribution. The bell curve with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\).


\(L = -\sum_i y_i \log \hat{y}_i\)
Cross-entropy loss. Penalises a model for giving low probability \(\hat{y}_i\) to the true class \(y_i\).


\(\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\,\nabla L(\theta)\)
Gradient descent. Moves parameters a small step \(\eta\) downhill on the loss; how most models are trained.


\(p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1\)
Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. Genotype frequencies for two alleles with frequencies \(p\) and \(q\) in a randomly mating population.


\(\hat{\beta} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y\)
Ordinary least squares. The linear-regression coefficients that minimise squared error.


\(\mathrm{Attn}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\dfrac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V\)
Attention. The core operation of transformer models: each position takes a weighted mix of values \(V\), weighted by how well queries \(Q\) match keys \(K\).


\(H(X) = -\sum_x p(x)\log p(x)\)
Shannon entropy. The average uncertainty, or information content, of a random variable.


\(y = X\beta + g + \varepsilon\)
Mixed model for genetics. A trait \(y\) explained by fixed effects \(X\beta\), a random genetic effect \(g\), and residual noise \(\varepsilon\).


\(\mathrm{KL}(p \,\Vert\, q) = \sum_x p(x)\log\dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}\)
Kullback–Leibler divergence. How much a distribution \(q\) differs from a reference distribution \(p\).


\(e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0\)
Euler’s identity. Ties together five fundamental constants (\(e\), \(i\), \(\pi\), 1 and 0) through complex exponentials; a special case of \(e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\).


\(\sigma(x) = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}\)
Sigmoid. Squashes any number into the range 0 to 1; used for probabilities and neuron activations.

title: Command-line basics: one-liners, aliases and SSH keys
text:
NoteFrom the archive



This merges three short posts from my old blog (Bash one-liners, text manipulation, Bash shells and aliases and Automatic SSH login, all February 2011). I have corrected a few mistakes in the originals and updated a few commands that have since changed. The corrections are listed at the end.

title: Command-line basics: one-liners, aliases and SSH keys
text:
Text one-liners
Bash is very powerful for text manipulation, and you can save a lot of time by learning a few short commands, the so-called one-liners.
To convert a string to upper case (or lower case), use tr:
echo "lowercase" | tr "[:lower:]" "[:upper:]"
# LOWERCASE
Two commands that are indispensable for any bioinformatician when checking large files are head and tail, which show the first or last N lines of a file:
head myfile.txt            # the first 10 lines
head -n 5 myfile.txt       # only the first 5 lines
tail -n 5 myfile.csv       # the last 5 lines
tail -n +2 myfile.csv      # everything from line 2 on (skips the header)
Now the really useful part: you can chain these commands with a pipe.
head -n 10 myfile.txt | tail -n 5   # lines 6 to 10
Quite often you need only a part of a line. Say you have the line Accuracy.mean=0.98 and you want just 0.98:
acc_mean=$(grep "Accuracy.mean" myfile.txt | awk -F= '{print $NF}')
And when a line contains unwanted spaces, here is the remedy:
echo "   I   a m    full of s p a ces  " | tr -d " "
# Iamfullofspaces

title: Command-line basics: one-liners, aliases and SSH keys
text:
Start-up files and aliases
Some commands are long and cumbersome to type, yet you need them several times a day. Aliases are a good remedy.
Each user has two important files in the home directory: .bash_profile and .bashrc. They are read by a login shell and a non-login shell, respectively. A login shell is the one you get when you log in; every shell you open after that is a non-login shell. Typically, commands you want to run only at login, such as displaying system or network information, go into .bash_profile, and everything else, including aliases, goes into .bashrc. To avoid repetition, end your .bash_profile by including .bashrc:
if [ -f ~/.bashrc ]; then
   source ~/.bashrc
fi
macOS users: Terminal opens a login shell every time, so it reads .bash_profile (or .zprofile/.zshrc if you use zsh, which is the default today).
Beginners’ note: file names that start with a dot, such as .bashrc, are hidden. You can see them with:
ls -al
Say you often use ls -alh, which lists all files, including hidden ones, with their sizes in human-readable form. To have something shorter, add this line to the end of your .bashrc:
alias ll='ls -alh'
From now on, typing ll gives you all the information about your files. After editing the profile files, re-open the shell (or run source ~/.bashrc) to use the aliases.
A useful maintenance alias on Debian or Ubuntu updates the whole system with one word:
alias admin='sudo apt update && sudo apt -y full-upgrade && sudo apt -y autoclean'

title: Command-line basics: one-liners, aliases and SSH keys
section: Logging in over SSH without a password
text:
Logging in over SSH without a password
If you log into a server over SSH several times a day, typing the password every time gets annoying. It is easy to set up key-based login. Suppose you want to allow your workstation to connect to the server. First, generate a key pair on the workstation:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519
and answer the questions: where to save the key, and an optional passphrase (a passphrase is a good idea). The command prints a fingerprint and a small picture, the key’s randomart:



The randomart image of an SSH key


The image is a visual representation of the key’s fingerprint. It is meant to be easier for humans to compare and verify than a string of hexadecimal characters, such as ef:f2:5b:9c:…. They are fun, anyway.
Now the public key has to be added to the list of trusted keys on the server. The simplest way is:
ssh-copy-id user@server
This creates ~/.ssh on the server if needed and appends your public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. If ssh-copy-id is not available, the same can be done by hand:
ssh user@server mkdir -p .ssh
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub | ssh user@server 'cat >> .ssh/authorized_keys'
You should now be able to log in without typing the password. If it still asks, check the permissions on the server: ~/.ssh should be 700 and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys should be 600 (or at least not writable by others).

title: Command-line basics: one-liners, aliases and SSH keys
text:
Corrections to the original posts

tail -n myfile.csv was missing the number; tail +2 is the obsolete form of tail -n +2.
head -n 10 … | tail -n 5 shows lines 6 to 10, not “5 to 10”.
awk '{FS="="}…' sets the separator too late for the first line; -F= is the right way.
The ll alias was announced as ls -alh but defined as ls -al; it is now ls -alh.
The admin alias used aptitude; it now uses apt.
The SSH key type was RSA (ssh-keygen -t rsa); ed25519 is the usual choice today, and ssh-copy-id replaces the manual steps.

title: Variance-controlling genes
text:
NoteFrom the archive



First published on my old blog in August 2012; lightly edited for this site.


The August 2012 issue of PLoS Genetics brought an interesting article by Xia Shen and colleagues from the Computational Genetics Section at the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences. They show that polymorphisms and mutations can affect not only the mean of a trait but also its variance.
After developing the necessary theory, the authors use an Arabidopsis thaliana dataset from Magnus Nordborg’s lab to pinpoint examples of such variance-controlling genes. It is clearly shown that the classical GWAS approach can completely miss genetic effects that influence trait variance. They propose an extended approach, called vGWAS, that helps discover variance-controlling genes.
Read it: Shen X, Pettersson M, Rönnegård L, Carlborg Ö (2012). Inheritance beyond plain heritability: variance-controlling genes in Arabidopsis thaliana. PLoS Genetics 8(8): e1002839. doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.1002839

title: Plotting 23andMe marker density with karyoploteR
text:
NoteUpdated in 2026



This is a lightly edited version of a 2018 post. The prose and figures are the originals. The code is updated for current Bioconductor, but it is shown, not re-run: the SNPedia files the post relied on are no longer downloadable, so the figures below are the ones produced in 2018.

title: Plotting 23andMe marker density with karyoploteR
text:
Background
23andMe is a personal genomics company that offers saliva-based, direct-to-consumer genetic testing. It is probably one of the most popular ways for people to learn more about their own genetic makeup, including ancestry.
For genotyping, the company uses a SNP array (SNP-chip). In short, such a chip lets us “read” polymorphic sites in human DNA: sites known to vary between individuals. Different versions of these sites are associated with traits such as eye colour, blood group or the risk of developing a disease. A given version does not always cause the phenotype. Often a SNP is a good proxy: it tags the phenotype. This works because DNA is inherited in rather long chunks (haplotypes), so a variant tends to travel together with its neighbours, including the actual causative variant. Thanks to this, genotyping a limited number of SNPs can tell you a lot about many traits.
23andMe has used three versions of its chip, introduced in 2008, 2012 and 2014. I was curious how they differ, so I wanted to visualise the density of genotyped SNPs per fixed-length window along the genome.

title: Plotting 23andMe marker density with karyoploteR
text:
The data
23andMe uses the Mendel family as its showcase. We look at the data for one family member, Lily Mendel (a real person: Linda Avey, a co-founder of the company). Data from all three chips were available at SNPedia (2008 v1, 2012 v3 and 2014 v4). The format is simple: one row per marker, with four columns:

rsid – unique rs identifier of the marker,
chr – chromosome,
pos – coordinate of the marker,
gtype – the genotype, e.g. GG.

title: Plotting 23andMe marker density with karyoploteR
text:
Analysis

Preparations

# install once:
# if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager")) install.packages("BiocManager")
# BiocManager::install(c("karyoploteR", "biomaRt"))

library(karyoploteR)



Loading the data
We load the data, fix the column names and convert it into a GRanges object, which is what the density plot needs.

gdata <- read.table(file = "genome_Lilly_Mendel_v4.txt", comment.char = "#")
names(gdata) <- c("rsid", "chr", "pos", "gtype")

regions <- GRanges(seqnames = paste0("chr", gdata$chr),
                   ranges = IRanges(start = gdata$pos, width = 2))



Plotting marker density
A karyogram is an ideogram of ordered chromosomes: a map of the genome. We plot marker density over each chromosome with kpPlotDensity(). A nice feature of karyoploteR is that it also draws the G-bands, the pattern produced by Giemsa staining, which cytogeneticists use to visualise chromosome structure. The one important parameter here is the window size, which I set empirically to 1 Mbp.

kp <- plotKaryotype(cex = .7) |>
  kpAddBaseNumbers(cex = .5) |>
  kpPlotDensity(data = regions,
                window.size = 1e6,
                col = "slateblue",
                border = "slateblue")




Density of genotyped markers (1 Mbp windows) along the human karyotype.




So what?
I think the visualisation is neat, although the y-axis is missing (we fix that next). We can see low marker density around centromeres (the central, red-stained parts of the chromosomes) and a long stretch with no markers on the Y chromosome, probably its non-pseudoautosomal region. The density is also very low at the start of chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21 and 22, and exceptionally high on the short arm of chromosome 6. I had no idea why, and not much time to research it…


Plotting the actual counts
What if we want the counts per window rather than the density? Easy enough:

counts <- kp$latest.plot$computed.values$density
data_counts <- GRanges(kp$latest.plot$computed.values$windows, y = counts)
max_count <- floor(max(counts) + .1 * max(counts))

# Plotting parameters established by trial and error
pp <- getDefaultPlotParams(plot.type = 1)
pp$leftmargin <- 0.15  # keep chromosome names clear of the plot
pp$topmargin <- 150    # avoid overlap between chromosomes
pp$bottommargin <- 150

kp <- plotKaryotype(cex = .7, plot.params = pp) |>
  kpAddBaseNumbers(cex = .5) |>
  kpLines(data = data_counts, ymin = 0, ymax = max_count) |>
  kpAxis(cex = .5, ymin = 0, ymax = max_count)




Marker counts per 1 Mbp window.


I did not manage to avoid all overlap between chromosomes and their data panels. It can probably be refined by playing with the graphical parameters, but you get the idea.


Zooming in
We spotted a region of high marker density on the short arm of chromosome 6. Let’s take a closer look.

pp <- getDefaultPlotParams(plot.type = 1)
pp$leftmargin <- 0.15
pp$topmargin <- 120
to_zoom <- GRanges("chr6", IRanges(start = 20e6, end = 60e6))

kp <- plotKaryotype(cex = .7, plot.params = pp, zoom = to_zoom) |>
  kpAddBaseNumbers(cex = .5) |>
  kpAxis(cex = .5, ymin = 0) |>
  kpBars(data = data_counts, y1 = data_counts$y, ymax = max_count)




Chromosome 6, 20-60 Mbp.


Almost perfect; only the y-axis has vanished in a mysterious way (my fault or a feature of the package, I never found out). The highest counts occur roughly between 30 and 35 Mbp. It would be interesting to see which genes sit there.






WarningWhat a real study would need




Check the exact coordinates of the dense region rather than eyeballing 30-35 Mbp.
23andMe uses hg19 coordinates, while current Ensembl uses hg38. The code below asks Ensembl for GRCh37 (= hg19) so the two agree. Otherwise you would lift the coordinates over, for instance with liftOver. I did that back then, and the regions were close enough not to matter for this post.



To find the attributes and filters available in BioMart, see the BioMart web interface; once you have set them, click XML.

library(biomaRt)

ensembl <- useEnsembl(biomart = "genes",
                      dataset = "hsapiens_gene_ensembl",
                      GRCh = 37)

genes <- getBM(attributes = c("ensembl_gene_id", "external_gene_name", "description"),
               filters = c("chromosome_name", "start", "end"),
               values = list("6", 30000000, 35000000),
               mart = ensembl)

knitr::kable(genes)

Now we know what sits in the region. Any guesses why 23andMe put so many markers there?

title: Statistics from the beginning: location and spread
text: Series · Statistics from the beginning · Part 1

title: Statistics from the beginning: location and spread
text:
Statistics, and a statistic
Statistics is a branch of mathematics concerned with the collection, analysis, interpretation and presentation of data. A very similar word, a statistic, means something narrower: a single number that summarises some feature of a data sample, produced by a statistical procedure. The sample mean and the sample standard deviation are statistics.
One distinction runs through everything that follows:

distributions (populations) are described by parameters,
samples are described by statistics.

We almost never see the whole population, so we use statistics computed from a sample to estimate the parameters of the distribution it came from. Every distribution can be described by two kinds of parameters: location parameters (where are the data?) and spread (dispersion) parameters (how widely is it scattered?).

library(ggplot2)

# A shared look for the figures in this series
accent <- "#8c2f39"; gold <- "#b08d4a"; ink <- "#5d6070"
theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#FFFDF8", colour = NA),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#EEEAE0", linewidth = 0.3),
          plot.title.position = "plot")
)

title: Statistics from the beginning: location and spread
text:
Location: where are the data?

Mean
The mean measures the central tendency of the data: the sum of all values divided by the number of observations,
\[
\mu = \frac{\sum x}{N}.
\]
The population mean is written \(\mu\) and the sample mean \(\bar{x}\); \(N\) is the number of observations.
The mean has a weakness: it uses every value, so it is pulled around by outliers and by skewed distributions. Five sheep weighing between 52 and 57 kg have a mean of 54.8 kg. Add one animal recorded as 120 kg (perhaps a typo) and see what happens:

sheep <- c(52, 54, 55, 56, 57)
c(mean = mean(sheep), median = median(sheep))

  mean median 
  54.8   55.0 

sheep_typo <- c(sheep, 120)
c(mean = mean(sheep_typo), median = median(sheep_typo))

    mean   median 
65.66667 55.50000 


The mean jumps by more than ten kilos; the median barely moves. People handle this problem with variants of the mean, such as the weighted mean or the Winsorised mean, which tames extreme observations, but we will not go into those here.


Median
The median is another location parameter. Unlike the mean it does not use all the observations: it is simply the middle value of the ordered data. With an odd number of data points it is easy to find. With an even number, it is the mean of the two middle values.
Comparing the mean with the median tells us something about skewness:

for a perfectly symmetric distribution, mean and median are equal,
for a right-skewed distribution (a long tail to the right), the mean is greater than the median, because the tail drags the mean along,
for a left-skewed distribution (a long tail to the left), the mean is less than the median.


set.seed(42)
x <- data.frame(value = rgamma(2000, shape = 2, rate = 0.5))

ggplot(x, aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 45, fill = "#d8cfba", colour = "#FFFDF8") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(x$value), colour = gold, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(x$value), colour = accent, linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = median(x$value) - 0.2, y = Inf, vjust = 2, hjust = 1,
           label = "median", colour = gold) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(x$value) + 0.2, y = Inf, vjust = 2, hjust = 0,
           label = "mean", colour = accent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "A right-skewed sample: mean > median")

title: Statistics from the beginning: location and spread
section: Spread: how scattered are the data?
text:
Spread: how scattered are the data?

Variance
Variance measures dispersion around the mean: the more spread out the observations, the larger the variance. The population variance is \(\sigma^2\) and the sample variance is \(s^2\):
\[
\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum (x - \mu)^2}{N}
\qquad\qquad
s^2 = \frac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}.
\]
Why divide by \(n - 1\) rather than \(n\)? We want \(s^2\) to be as good an estimate of \(\sigma^2\) as possible. Think of estimating the variance of weights in a herd of 2,000 sheep from a sample of 200. It is quite likely that our sample misses the few very light and very heavy animals, which would otherwise have contributed large \((x - \bar{x})^2\) terms. There is a second, more precise way to see it: we measure the deviations from \(\bar{x}\), a number computed from the same sample, and the sample is always closer to its own mean than to the true mean \(\mu\). Dividing by \(n\) would therefore underestimate the variance systematically; dividing by \(n - 1\) corrects it exactly.
Let’s check this with a simulation. We create a herd of 2,000 sheep, draw many samples of each size, and compare the two estimators with the true population variance.

set.seed(2017)
herd <- rnorm(2000, mean = 55, sd = 4)

# population variance: divide by N
pop_var <- function(x) sum((x - mean(x))^2) / length(x)
true_var <- pop_var(herd)

compare_var <- function(pop, n_draws, sample_size) {
  draws <- replicate(n_draws, sample(pop, sample_size))   # one sample per column
  c(corrected   = mean(apply(draws, 2, var)),             # divides by n - 1
    uncorrected = mean(apply(draws, 2, pop_var)))         # divides by n
}

sizes <- 5:100
sim <- t(sapply(sizes, function(n) compare_var(herd, 1000, n)))
sim <- data.frame(n = rep(sizes, 2),
                  estimate = c(sim[, "uncorrected"], sim[, "corrected"]),
                  version = rep(c("divide by n", "divide by n − 1"), each = length(sizes)))


ggplot(sim, aes(n, estimate, colour = version)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = true_var, colour = ink, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("divide by n" = "#2b2117", "divide by n − 1" = accent)) +
  labs(x = "Sample size", y = "Average estimated variance", colour = NULL,
       title = "The effect of using n − 1 in the denominator",
       subtitle = "Dotted line: true population variance, averaged over 1,000 samples per size") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








For small samples, dividing by \(n\) clearly underestimates the variance; for large samples the choice hardly matters, because \(n\) and \(n - 1\) are nearly the same number.
Variance can never be negative, since we square the deviations. A side effect of that squaring is that variance is expressed in squared units (kilograms squared for weights). That is why we usually report its square root instead.


Standard deviation
The standard deviation (sd, SD, std. dev.) is the square root of the variance, written \(\sigma\) for a population and \(s\) for a sample. It is in the same units as the data, which makes it far easier to interpret: for our sheep, an sd of about 4 means that a typical animal is within a few kilograms of the herd’s mean weight.


Putting different scales on the same footing
If two traits are measured on different scales (say, body weight in kilograms and fleece length in centimetres), their variances cannot be compared directly: the numbers depend on the units. The usual remedy is standardisation: we transform each variable so that it has mean 0 and standard deviation 1, i.e. it follows the standard normal scale \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\). The standardised values are called z-scores; each one tells us how many standard deviations an observation lies from the mean:
\[
z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s}.
\]

set.seed(7)
herd2 <- data.frame(weight_kg = rnorm(200, 55, 4),
                    fleece_cm = rnorm(200, 11, 1.5))

ewe <- c(weight_kg = 58, fleece_cm = 13.4)
z <- (ewe - colMeans(herd2)) / sapply(herd2, sd)
round(z, 2)

weight_kg fleece_cm 
     0.65      1.56 


On the raw scale, 58 kg and 13.4 cm cannot be compared. As z-scores they can: this hypothetical ewe is about two-thirds of a standard deviation heavier than average, but more than one and a half standard deviations above average in fleece length. Relative to the rest of the herd, her fleece is the more unusual feature.

title: Research
text: My work sits between biology, statistics and computer science. Most of it is collaborative: as a data scientist in a national infrastructure, I work with groups across Sweden, from veterinary medicine to evolutionary biology to clinical research.

title: Research
text:
Themes

Statistical and complex-trait genomics
Mixed-model and gene-based approaches for finding the variants behind disease and quantitative traits, including rare variants and missing heritability. Examples include chronic kidney disease in boxers, atopic dermatitis in German shepherds, pyometra in golden retrievers and plasma protein levels in humans.

Selected papers

Contribution of rare whole-genome sequencing variants to plasma protein levels and the missing heritability. Nature Communications, 2022.
Bayesian mixed model analysis uncovered 21 risk loci for chronic kidney disease in boxer dogs. PLOS Genetics, 2023.
The ABCC4 gene is associated with pyometra in golden retriever dogs. Scientific Reports, 2021.




Conservation and ancient genomics
Population genomics of endangered and extinct mammals, such as the Sumatran and woolly rhinoceros, and the pipeline GenErode for quantifying genome erosion.

Selected papers

Genomic insights into the conservation status of the world’s last remaining Sumatran rhinoceros populations. Nature Communications, 2021.
Pre-extinction Demographic Stability and Genomic Signatures of Adaptation in the Woolly Rhinoceros. Current Biology, 2020.
GenErode: a bioinformatics pipeline to investigate genome erosion in endangered and extinct species. BMC Bioinformatics, 2022.




Cancer genomics
Somatic variation in canine osteosarcoma (SETD2) and structural variants in multiple myeloma resolved with linked-read sequencing.

Selected papers

SETD2 Is Recurrently Mutated in Whole-Exome Sequenced Canine Osteosarcoma. Cancer Research, 2018.
Linked-read whole-genome sequencing resolves common and private structural variants in multiple myeloma. Blood Advances, 2022.




Machine learning for biology
Ensemble learning for protein–protein interaction prediction, rough-set classifiers for HIV-1 drug resistance, and modern neural-network methods for omics data.

Selected papers

Ensemble learning prediction of protein–protein interactions using proteins functional annotations. Molecular BioSystems, 2014.
A Rough Set-Based Model of HIV-1 Reverse Transcriptase Resistome. Bioinformatics and Biology Insights, 2009.




Metagenomics and metabarcoding
DNA metabarcoding for authenticating food products, and genome assembly from single nuclei of complex microorganisms.

Selected papers

DNA Metabarcoding for Quality Control of Basil, Oregano, and Paprika. Frontiers in Plant Science, 2021.
Building de novo reference genome assemblies of complex eukaryotic microorganisms from single nuclei. Scientific Reports, 2020.
